title: Why probability needs measure
objectives: See why not every set can have a probability, with a uniform pick from an interval.

screens.title: A uniform pick
screens.prose: Topic 3.2 is optional: it serves desk quant and derivatives pricing roles. A number $X$ is picked uniformly from $[0, 1]$, so a chance is a length. The bars show $[0.2, 0.5]$ and a window of half-width 0.1 round 0.5.
screens.question: Fill in each chance.

hints.text: A chance is a length, so measure each bar.
The first bar runs from 0.2 to 0.5. The window runs from $0.5 - h$ to $0.5 + h$.

feedback.correct: 0.3, 0.2 and 0.02: each chance is a length, and the window has length $2h$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the left end from the right end of each bar.

byKey.r1c1: A window of half-width 0.1 has length $0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2$. You gave the half-width.
byKey.r2c1: A window of half-width 0.01 has length 0.02, twice the half-width.

explain.text: A uniform pick gives each interval a chance equal to its length. So $[0.2, 0.5]$ has 0.3 and a window of half-width $h$ has $2h$.

screens.title: A window that shrinks
screens.prose: Slide the half-width $h$ down towards 0. The window closes on the single point 0.5.

derive.caption: Window width $2h$ = {{fixed(2 * h, 3)}}, so its chance is {{fixed(2 * h, 3)}}.

screens.question: What is $P(X = 0.5)$?

widget.accept: 0: the window has chance $2h$ for every $h$
widget.label: Chance

hints.text: The point sits inside every window.
The point has at most the chance of each window, and the windows shrink to 0.
$P(X = 0.5) \le 2h$ for every $h > 0$, so it is 0.

feedback.correct: 0. The point is inside every window, and the windows have chance $2h$ for every $h$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the point with a window of half-width 0.001, then a smaller one.

byKey.tiny: A window of half-width 0.0004 has chance 0.0008, and the point lies inside it. So $P(X = 0.5) \le 0.0008$, and no positive number works.

explain.text: The point lies inside every window, and $2h$ can be as small as we like. So $P(X = 0.5) = 0$, and the same holds for every point. Yet $X$ lands on some point, and the axioms add only countably many chances.

screens.title: Covering the rationals
screens.prose: List the rationals of $[0, 1]$ by denominator: $0, 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \tfrac23, \dots$. Cover the $k$th with an interval of length $\varepsilon / 2^k$. Slide $\varepsilon$ and watch the cover shrink.
screens.question: Set $\varepsilon = 0.01$. How long are the first ten intervals in all? Give 5 decimal places.

hints.text: The lengths are $0.01/2, 0.01/4, 0.01/8, \dots$
Add ten terms of a geometric series with first term 0.005 and ratio $\tfrac12$.

feedback.correct: 0.00999: ten terms of the series fall just short of the full total 0.01.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sum $\tfrac{0.01}{2^k}$ for $k = 1$ to 10, not for every $k$.

byKey.full: 0.01 is the total of all the intervals, with no end. Ten intervals leave out the tail $0.01/2^{10}$.

explain.text: The ten lengths are $\tfrac{0.01}{2}, \tfrac{0.01}{4}, \dots, \tfrac{0.01}{1024}$. Their sum is $0.01(1 - 2^{-10}) = \tfrac{1023}{102400}$. All of them together add to exactly 0.01.

screens.title: Why the rationals have chance 0
screens.prose: Now take all the intervals, one for every rational. Together they cover $\mathbb{Q} \cap [0, 1]$, and their lengths add to $\varepsilon$.
screens.question: Which argument shows $P(X \in \mathbb{Q}) = 0$?

options.text: The cover holds $\mathbb{Q}$, so $P(\mathbb{Q}) \le \sum_k \varepsilon/2^k = \varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon$.
The intervals have chance $\varepsilon / 2^k$, so $P(\mathbb{Q})$ equals their sum, $\varepsilon$.
options.why: You treated the cover as $\mathbb{Q}$ itself. It only contains $\mathbb{Q}$, so it gives an upper bound.

options.text: The rationals are dense, so every window holds one, and $P(\mathbb{Q}) = 1$ as a result.
options.why: You used density. A set can meet every window and still have tiny length.

options.text: Each point has chance 0, so any set of points has chance 0, whatever its size.
options.why: You added chances over any set of points. Countable additivity covers a list of points, not uncountably many.

hints.text: The cover contains every rational.
Use monotonicity, then countable additivity on the lengths.
$P(\mathbb{Q}) \le \sum_k \varepsilon / 2^k = \varepsilon$.

feedback.correct: The cover has length at most $\varepsilon$, and $\varepsilon$ is as small as we like. So $P(\mathbb{Q}) = 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The cover contains $\mathbb{Q}$, so ask what monotonicity and countable additivity say about it.

byKey.b: The cover is bigger than $\mathbb{Q}$, so $\varepsilon$ is only a bound.
byKey.d: Uncountable sums of zeros are not defined by the axioms.

explain.text: Monotonicity gives $P(\mathbb{Q}) \le P(\text{cover})$. Countable subadditivity bounds that by $\varepsilon$. As $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, $P(\mathbb{Q}) = 0$, and the irrationals have chance 1.

screens.title: The Cantor set
screens.prose: Start with $[0, 1]$. At each stage remove the open middle third of every interval left. Slide through stages 0 to 4.
screens.question: After 10 stages, how much length is left? Give 7 decimal places.

hints.text: Each stage keeps two thirds of the length.
Stage $n$ has length $(2/3)^n$ in $2^n$ intervals.

feedback.correct: 0.0173415, in 1,024 intervals. The length goes to 0 as the stages go on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each stage multiplies the length by $\tfrac23$.

byKey.third: You removed two thirds each stage. We remove one third, so two thirds remain.
byKey.half: You halved the length. Each stage keeps two thirds, not one half.

explain.text: Each stage keeps two thirds of the length, so stage 10 has $(2/3)^{10} \approx 0.0173415$ in $2^{10} = 1024$ intervals. The length tends to 0, so the Cantor set has chance 0 under the uniform pick. It still has uncountably many points.

screens.title: A set with no length
screens.prose: Call $x \sim y$ when $x - y$ is rational. This sorts $[0, 1)$ into classes. Choose one point from each class (the axiom of choice) and call the set $V$. Shift $V$ by a rational $q$, wrapping round at 1: this is $V_q$.
screens.question: Why do $V_q$ and $V_r$ share no point when $q \ne r$?

options.text: A shared point gives two points of $V$ differing by the rational $q - r$. One point per class forces $q = r$.
A shift moves every point, so a point of $V_q$ can never be a point of $V_r$, whichever shifts we use.
options.why: You compared a shifted point with itself. A point of $V_q$ may land on a point of $V_r$ unless something forbids it.

options.text: There are countably many rationals and $V$ is uncountable, so the shifted copies cannot meet.
options.why: Counting the shifts says nothing about overlaps. Overlap is a question about points.

options.text: $V$ has length 0, so every shift of it is empty and no two copies can share a point.
options.why: You used the answer we are looking for. We do not yet know that $V$ has a length.

hints.text: Suppose a point $x$ lies in both $V_q$ and $V_r$.
Then $x - q$ and $x - r$ are both points of $V$.
They differ by $r - q$, which is rational, so they share a class.

feedback.correct: A shared point would put two points of $V$ in one class, which $V$ forbids.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Suppose a point lies in both sets, and see which two points of $V$ it gives.

byKey.b: Nothing says a shifted point cannot land on another shifted point.
byKey.c: Overlap is about points, not counts.
byKey.d: We cannot assume $V$ has a length.

explain.text: Suppose $x \in V_q \cap V_r$. Then $x - q$ and $x - r$ are points of $V$ that differ by $r - q$, a rational. They sit in one class, so they are the same point, and $q = r$.

screens.title: The Vitali argument
screens.prose: Assume a length $m$ exists for every subset of $[0, 1)$ and a shift keeps it. Assemble the argument. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order, a reason in each line. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Sort $[0, 1)$ into classes of points that differ by a rational. Choose one point from each class to make $V$.
For each rational $q$ in $[0, 1)$, let $V_q$ be $V$ shifted by $q$, wrapping round at 1.
The $V_q$ are disjoint: a shared point puts two points of $V$ in one class.
The $V_q$ cover $[0, 1)$: any $x$ is within a rational of its class's point in $V$.
A shift keeps length, so every $V_q$ has the same length $m$, and countable additivity gives $1 = m + m + \cdots$.
If $m = 0$ the sum is 0, and if $m > 0$ it is infinite. Neither is 1, so $V$ has no length.
The sum has two values at once, so $V$ has length $\tfrac12$.
lines.why: You split the difference. A sum of equal terms is 0 or infinite, and never $\tfrac12$.

lines.text: There are uncountably many shifts, so additivity fails.
lines.why: You counted the shifts wrongly. The rationals are countable, which is why additivity applies.

feedback.correct: Right. No length can be countably additive, shift-invariant and defined on every subset.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The sum needs the shifts disjoint and covering first.

byKey.d1: You used the line giving $\tfrac12$. Equal terms add to 0 or to infinity.
byKey.d2: You used the line about uncountably many shifts. The rationals in $[0, 1)$ are countable.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the argument needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

hints.text: First build $V$, then the shifts, then check disjoint and cover, then add.
The disjoint and cover lines are independent, and both come before the sum.
Order: choose $V$, shift, disjoint and cover (either way round), sum, contradiction.

explain.text: The shifts split $[0, 1)$ into countably many pieces of one length $m$. Countable additivity then gives $1 = m + m + \cdots$, which no $m$ satisfies. So some sets cannot have a probability, and we choose which ones can (next lesson).

screens.title: Chance 0 means impossible?
screens.prose: A colleague watches the uniform pick. They say 0.5 can never come up, because $P(X = 0.5) = 0$.
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: 0.5 can come up. Every value has chance 0, and one of them does.
They are right: chance 0 means the value cannot happen.
options.why: You read chance 0 as impossible. Every value has chance 0, yet $X$ takes one of them.

options.text: 0.5 is special. The other values have a positive chance.
options.why: You singled out 0.5. The window argument gives chance 0 to every point the same way.

options.text: 0.5 will come up about once in a million picks.
options.why: You gave 0.5 a chance of one in a million. That is positive, and a million such values would already add to 1.

hints.text: Run the window argument at a different point, such as 0.3.
Every point has chance 0, but the picks do land somewhere.
Chance 0 allows an outcome that is possible. The empty set is only one of the events with chance 0.

feedback.correct: Right. An event of chance 0 can still happen: it is just never the one you named in advance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the window argument to any other value.

byKey.d: A positive chance for each point would sum past 1.

explain.text: Every window round any point has chance $2h$, so every point has chance 0. A pick still lands on one of them. Chance 0 means 'almost never', not 'never'.

screens.title: Rationals, covers and the Cantor set in code
screens.prose: Write three exact functions with `Fraction`. `first_rationals(k)` lists the first $k$ rationals of $[0, 1]$ in the order above. `cover_length(eps, k)` adds the first $k$ cover lengths. `cantor_left(n)` gives the length left at stage $n$.
screens.question: Complete all three functions.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests with exact fractions. Four test first_rationals (the first ten, the 7th, the 30th and a slice), three test cover_length and three test cantor_left.

hints.text: Loop over denominators $d = 2, 3, \dots$ and numerators $1$ to $d - 1$.
Keep a fraction only when `gcd(n, d) == 1`. Start the list with 0 and 1.
`cover_length` is `sum(Fraction(eps) / 2**j for j in range(1, k + 1))`. `cantor_left` is `Fraction(2, 3) ** n`.

feedback.correct: Right. The listing, the cover length and the Cantor length all match as exact fractions.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Return `Fraction` values and keep only fractions in lowest terms.

explain.text: `first_rationals` walks the denominators and skips fractions not in lowest terms, since they were listed earlier. The cover length is a finite geometric sum, and the Cantor length is a power of $\tfrac23$.

screens.title: Two digitals, one price or two
screens.prose: A digital pays £1 if $S_T \ge K$ and a second pays £1 if $S_T > K$. Under a lognormal price $P(S_T = K) = 0$, so both cost $e^{-0.05}\Phi(0.15) = $ £0.5323. Now take a tree with $u = 1.25$, $d = 0.8$, $r = 5\%$ per step and two steps: $q = \tfrac59$.
screens.question: Strike $K = 100$. How much more does the $\ge$ digital cost than the $>$ digital on this tree? Give £ to 4 places.

hints.text: Only the paths ending at exactly £100 differ between the two digitals.
Two paths end at £100: up then down, and down then up. Each has chance $\tfrac59 \times \tfrac49$.

feedback.correct: £0.4479. On a tree the point $S_T = K$ has chance $\tfrac{40}{81}$, so the two digitals differ.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price the extra payoff: £1 on the paths that end exactly at £100, discounted twice.

byKey.same: You used the lognormal answer. On a tree $S_T = K$ has positive chance, so the prices differ.
byKey.ge: That is the price of the $\ge$ digital. You are asked for the difference.
byKey.gt: That is the price of the $>$ digital. You are asked for the difference.

explain.text: The $\ge$ digital also pays at £100, which two paths reach with total chance $\tfrac{40}{81}$. Discounted twice at 5% that is £0.4479. Prices: £0.7279 and £0.2799.

ideas: A uniform pick gives every point chance 0, yet it lands on one. Chance 0 is not impossible.
The axioms add countably many chances. The rationals are countable, so they have chance 0 and the irrationals have chance 1.
The Vitali set shows no length works on every subset. So probability lives on a chosen family of events.

formula.name: Countable additivity
formula.tex: P\Big(\bigcup_{k} A_k\Big) = \sum_k P(A_k) \text{ for disjoint } A_k
formula.note: A list of events, never uncountably many.

summary.trap: Chance 0 does not mean the event cannot happen.

quiz.prose: A number $X$ is picked uniformly from $[0, 1]$.
quiz.question: What is $P(X \text{ is irrational})$?

options.why: You gave the chance of a rational pick. The rationals have chance 0, and the irrationals are the rest.
You split the numbers into two equal halves. The rationals are countable and have length 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The rationals and irrationals together fill $[0, 1]$, and the rationals have chance 0.

explain.text: $P(\mathbb{Q}) = 0$ and $P([0, 1]) = 1$, so the irrationals have chance 1.

widget.accept: 0.3: open and closed ends differ by two points, each of chance 0
widget.label: Chance

feedback.correct: 0.3. The two end points have chance 0, so open and closed ends agree.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare with $P(0.2 \le X \le 0.5)$ and the chance of the two end points.

explain.text: $P(0.2 \le X \le 0.5) = 0.3$, and removing two points of chance 0 changes nothing.

options.text: No. Its points match binary sequences, which cannot be listed.
Yes, a set of length 0 is small enough to be listed.
options.why: You moved from length 0 to countable. The Cantor set has length 0 and is uncountable.

options.text: Yes, it is made of the end points of removed intervals.
options.why: You counted only the end points, which are countable. The set holds many more points.

feedback.correct: No. Length 0 does not mean countable.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of the Cantor set as all sequences of 0s and 2s, and recall the diagonal argument.

explain.text: Each point of the Cantor set is a ternary string of 0s and 2s. These match binary strings one for one, and the diagonal argument shows binary strings cannot be listed.

quiz.prose: The Vitali set $V$ picks one point from each class of $x \sim y$ when $x - y$ is rational.
quiz.question: What does the argument about its shifts show?

options.text: No length on all subsets can be countably additive and shift-invariant.
The set $V$ has length $\tfrac12$, the average of the two sums 0 and $\infty$.
options.why: You averaged 0 and infinity. The sum is 0 or infinite, never $\tfrac12$.

options.text: The rationals have length 1, as they are dense in $[0, 1)$, so the classes fill it.
options.why: You mixed the classes with the rationals. The classes use rational shifts, and the rationals have length 0.

feedback.correct: Some subsets must be left without a chance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which property of length gives $1 = m + m + \cdots$.

explain.text: Equal lengths over countably many disjoint shifts that cover $[0, 1)$ cannot add to 1. So we keep only some sets as events.
